title: Iran Launches 2 Ballistic Missiles and 3 Drones at UAE — All 5 Intercepted, 3 Wounded — Day 70
detail: Iran launched two ballistic missiles and three drones at the United Arab Emirates on May 8, 2026 — Day 70 — the second significant Iranian strike on UAE territory in four days (following the May 5 oil facility attack). UAE air defenses intercepted all five incoming projectiles. Three people were wounded with moderate injuries from debris or blast effects. The UAE Defense Ministry confirmed the interceptions and condemned the attack, demanding an international response. The repeated strikes on UAE demonstrated Iran's continued offensive pressure on Gulf states even during the nominal ceasefire period and simultaneous diplomatic negotiations on the MOU framework. Iran International reported the IRGC framed the strikes as a response to continued UAE hosting of US military assets used to support the Hormuz escort mission and naval blockade. NPR confirmed the barrage in a May 8 update covering the overall day's developments.

media.caption: Iran launches 2 ballistic missiles and 3 drones at the UAE on Day 70 — all intercepted, 3 wounded — second major strike on UAE in four days

title: US and Iran Exchange Fire in Strait of Hormuz Overnight — US Conducts Additional 'Self-Defense' Strikes; Iran Calls It Ceasefire Violation — Day 70
detail: US and Iranian forces exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz overnight during the night of May 7–8, 2026 — Day 70 — as the fragile nominal ceasefire continued to fray. US forces conducted additional 'self-defense' strikes against Iranian targets in or near the strait following Iranian fire. Iran's Foreign Ministry called the US strikes 'a clear violation' of the April 8 ceasefire and stated Iran 'will never bow to pressure.' Trump insisted the ceasefire was 'still in effect' despite the exchanges, arguing the US actions were defensive responses to Iranian aggression. UKMTO (United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations) reported attacks on two ships in the region during the May 8 period, consistent with the elevated threat environment. Approximately 1,600 ships remained stranded in and near the strait, with nearly 23,000 sailors from 87 countries trapped in the Persian Gulf — the human cost of the blockade now approaching 70 days. The overnight exchange demonstrated that even as both sides talked, military escalation remained an ever-present risk.

media.caption: US-Iran clash in Hormuz overnight May 7–8 — US conducts 'self-defense' strikes; Iran calls it ceasefire violation; ~1,600 ships stranded, 23,000 sailors trapped

title: Iran's Formal Response to US MOU Awaited — Rubio Expected Reply by May 8; Iran's Parliament Hostile; Deal Odds Rising on Markets — Day 70
detail: The central diplomatic development on May 8, 2026 — Day 70 — was the continued waiting for Iran's formal response to the US memorandum of understanding (MOU) framework. Rubio had expected Iran's reply by the end of May 8. Araghchi confirmed Iran was 'finalising its views' but had not yet delivered a response. CNN's live blog captured US officials saying they hoped for a 'serious offer from Iran.' Kalshi prediction markets showed rising odds — tracked by CNBC — that a US-Iran nuclear deal would be reached by 2027, reflecting growing market optimism about the MOU framework. Iran's parliament remained openly hostile: the Speaker Ghalibaf mocked the process, and a parliamentary spokesperson called the US framework 'more of an American wish-list than a reality.' Iran's core sticking point was Hormuz sequencing and sovereignty — Tehran insisted the strait's blockade must be lifted first, before any nuclear commitments, while Rubio had explicitly stated the US 'cannot accept paying a toll or coordinating with Iran' for Hormuz passage. Chinese banking regulators separately advised major banks to halt new loans to US-sanctioned Iranian-linked refineries — adding pressure on Iran's economy. The MOU's notable omissions (ballistic missiles, proxy networks) and Iran's insistence on reparations remained the principal gaps.

media.caption: Iran's formal MOU response awaited on Day 70 — Rubio expected reply by May 8; Kalshi markets show rising deal odds; Iran parliament hostile

title: 1,600 Ships Stranded, 23,000 Sailors Trapped — Day 70 Hormuz Crisis: 'Will Take a Long Time to Reboot'
detail: By Day 70 (May 8, 2026), approximately 1,600 ships remained stranded in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with nearly 23,000 sailors from 87 countries trapped in the Persian Gulf — one of the largest maritime hostage crises in modern history. NBC News reported that even after a potential deal is reached, the strait 'will take a long time to reboot' due to the logistics of clearing the shipping backlog, restoring insurance coverage, and restarting port operations. Hapag-Lloyd estimated the blockade was costing approximately $60 million per week in additional fuel and insurance costs alone. The UK Parliament's House of Commons Library published a research briefing on the challenges of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, reflecting the complexity of any post-deal normalization. UKMTO reported attacks on two ships on May 8. The 70-day closure of the world's most critical oil chokepoint — through which approximately 20–21 million barrels of oil pass per day in normal conditions — had cumulatively cost global economies an estimated $400+ billion in direct supply disruption.

media.caption: Day 70: 1,600 ships stranded, 23,000 sailors from 87 countries trapped in Persian Gulf — NBC News: Hormuz 'will take a long time to reboot' even after a deal
